```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(PGViS)
```

Now we combine the model probabilities with the allele frequencies into
per-variant metrics, and filter down to the variants that are both disruptive
and worth scoring. This whole step runs against the bundled fixture, so every
chunk here executes.

## The three metrics

Each (region, variant) pair gets three numbers, capturing complementary
evidence.

**Log-odds ratio** — how much the model's confidence in the regulatory element
drops when the variant is introduced. Positive means disruptive.

```{r lor}
log_odds_ratio(p_ref = 0.97, p_alt = 0.03)
log_odds_ratio(0.5, 0.5)          # no change -> 0
```

Probabilities are clamped away from 0 and 1, so a saturated prediction gives a
large finite number rather than infinity — which keeps a single confident
variant from poisoning a downstream mean.

**Score change** — a probability difference weighted by the larger of the two
probabilities, so a change between two low-confidence values counts for less.

```{r sc}
score_change(0.9, 0.7)    # confident, so the shift counts
score_change(0.3, 0.1)    # same 0.2 shift, but low confidence, so shrunk
```

**Delta-Wi** — divergence between the cohort allele frequencies and the matched
population frequencies. A variant enriched in the cohort relative to the
population scores high. It's rank-based inverse-normal transformed, because the
raw statistic is heavily right-skewed.

```{r dwi}
d <- data.frame(af_ref = 0.60, af_alt = 0.40,
                pop_af_ref = 0.95, pop_af_alt = 0.05)
pgvis_delta_wi(d, transform = FALSE, keep_raw = TRUE)[, c("delta_af_alt", "delta_wi")]
```

## Population frequency resolution

Delta-Wi needs a population frequency, and getting it out of dbSNP is fiddly:
UCSC packs each project's frequencies into one comma-delimited string, and you
have to find the project whose reported minor allele matches your variant.
PGViS walks the projects in priority order.

```{r popaf}
row <- data.frame(
  dbsnp_freqs = paste(c("0.11", "", "0.13", rep("", 9), "0.19"), collapse = ","),
  dbsnp_minor = paste(c("A",    "", "A",    rep("", 9), "A"),    collapse = ","),
  dbsnp_ref = "G", dbsnp_alt = "A"
)
pgvis_resolve_population_af(row)[, c("pop_af_alt", "pop_af_ref", "freq_source")]
```

The priority order is an argument, so you can prefer a different project when
more than one reports a frequency:

```{r popaf-priority}
pgvis_resolve_population_af(row, priority = c("1000G", "TOPMED"))$freq_source
```

When no project's minor allele matches, the result is `NA` and
`freq_source == "none"` — never a guess.

## Putting it together

`pgvis_variant_metrics()` joins the variant table to the predictions and
computes all three metrics in one call.

```{r metrics}
variants <- pgvis_example("variants")
preds    <- pgvis_example("predictions")

metrics <- pgvis_variant_metrics(variants, preds)
metrics[1:3, c("feature", "log_odds_ratio", "score_change", "delta_wi_int")]
```

The join is on `feature`, `func_site` and `var_site` — the canonical keys, so
there's no rename dance and no silent mismatch. Variants with no matching
prediction are reported and dropped.

## Filtering to disruptive variants

Not every scored variant is interesting. `pgvis_filter_disruptive()` keeps
those where the model is confident the reference is functional and the mutant
is not, and where enough samples carry the variant to matter.

```{r filter}
kept <- pgvis_filter_disruptive(
  metrics,
  ref_prob_min = 0.5, alt_prob_max = 0.5, min_carrier_frac = 0
)
nrow(metrics)
nrow(kept)
```

It records how many rows each criterion removed, so you can see where your
variants went:

```{r audit}
attr(kept, "pgvis_filter")
```

In a real run you'd pass `cfg` and let it use the configured thresholds (a
strict setting uses 0.7 / 0.3) rather than spelling them out each time.

## Quality control

Run `pgvis_qc()` before going further. It reports the things that most often
turn out to be wrong: features with no variants, missing population
frequencies, model probabilities that never move, and carrier counts that look
like a parsing artefact.

```{r qc}
pgvis_qc(metrics)
```

The two findings worth stopping for: a majority of variants with
`freq_source == "none"` (a dbSNP build mismatch), and degenerate predictions
(the model isn't distinguishing anything). Both come with an explanatory
warning rather than a bare number.

## Cross-study replication

A variant seen in both TCGA and CPTAC is far more credible than one seen in
either alone. When you've combined per-cohort results, this keeps only the
replicated sites — required *within* stratum, so a smoker hit and a non-smoker
hit don't count as replicating each other.

```{r replication}
combined <- data.frame(
  study     = c("tcga", "cptac", "tcga"),
  cancer    = "luad",
  func_site = c("f1", "f1", "f2"),
  var_site  = c("v1", "v1", "v2"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
pgvis_filter_replicated(combined, within = "cancer", min_studies = 2)
```

## What can go wrong

- **Everything filtered out.** Usually thresholds too strict for your data, or
  a QC problem upstream. The filter audit tells you which criterion did it.
- **`freq_source` mostly "none".** dbSNP build mismatch; the frequency-column
  indices in `pgvis_freq_sources()` are pinned to UCSC dbSnp155.
- **Metrics all `NA` for delta-Wi.** No population frequency resolved for those
  variants, so there's nothing to diverge from.
